content: A nevus, also known as a birthmark or beauty mark, is a sharply defined and chronic lesion of the skin or mucosa. These lesions are benign by definition, but approximately 25% of malignant melanomas, a type of skin cancer, originate from pre-existing nevi. When physicians or dermatologists refer to nevi, they are often discussing melanocytic nevi, which are composed of melanocytes, the cells responsible for producing melanin, the pigment that gives skin its color. Histologically, melanocytic nevi are differentiated from lentigines, another type of benign pigmented lesion, by the presence of nests of melanocytes, which are absent in lentigines. Classification of Nevi: 1. Epidermal Nevi: These are derived from keratinocytes or their derivatives. 2. Connective Tissue Nevi: These originate from connective tissue cells such as adipocytes or fibroblasts. 3. Vascular Nevi: These are derived from blood vessel structures. Types of Melanocytic Nevi: Congenital Nevus: A melanocytic nevus present at or near birth. Acquired Melanocytic Nevus: A melanocytic nevus that develops later in life, typically during puberty. Most melanocytic nevi fall into this category. Melanocytic Nevus (Nevomelanocytic or Nevocellular Nevus): This is a benign proliferation of melanocytes, resulting in lesions that are typically brown to black in color. These are extremely common, with nearly all adults having at least one. Dysplastic Nevus: This is usually an acquired melanocytic nevus with atypical features that make it challenging to distinguish from melanoma. It can serve as a marker for individuals at higher risk of developing melanoma. Types of Epidermal Nevi: Epidermal Nevus: A congenital lesion that is flesh-colored, raised, or warty in appearance, often arranged in a linear pattern and typically located on the upper half of the body. Nevus Sebaceous: A variant of epidermal nevus that appears on the scalp as a hairless, fleshy, or yellowish area. Darier-Like Epidermal Nevus: A specific subtype of epidermal nevus with features resembling Darier disease. Connective Tissue Nevus: These are rare, fleshy, deep nodules that originate from connective tissue. Vascular Nevus: Hemangioma: Commonly referred to as a strawberry mark, this is a type of vascular nevus. Diagnosis of Nevi: The clinical diagnosis of a melanocytic nevus can often be made visually using the ABCD guideline (Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color variation, Diameter) or with dermatoscopy. The primary concern is distinguishing between a benign nevus, a dysplastic nevus, and melanoma. Other skin lesions, such as seborrheic keratosis, pigmented basal cell carcinoma, hemangiomas, and sebaceous hyperplasia, can mimic melanocytic nevi. When the clinical diagnosis is uncertain or malignancy is suspected, a skin biopsy is necessary. Normal Evolution or Maturation of Melanocytic Nevi: Both congenital and acquired melanocytic nevi undergo changes over time. The typical maturation process involves the lesion transitioning from a flat macule to a raised papule. The color of the nevus changes as melanocytes cluster and migrate from the epidermis to the dermis. Initially, the lesion may appear uniformly brown, then develop a speckled appearance, and eventually lose pigmentation, becoming flesh-colored or pink. During this process, uneven migration of melanocytes can cause the nevus to resemble melanoma. Dermatoscopy is a valuable tool for differentiating between benign and malignant lesions during this evolution.
